title: What a share is
objectives: Explain shares, dividends and market capitalisation.
Value a share with the dividend discount model, and say when it breaks

screens.title: A slice of a company
screens.prose: A company is split into 10 million equal shares. You own 100,000 of them. This year it made a profit of £5 million after paying its costs, its lenders and its tax.
screens.question: How much of this year's profit belongs to your shares?

widget.label: Your part of the profit
widget.accept: £50,000: 1% of the shares, so 1% of the profit.

hints.text: What fraction of all the shares do you own?

feedback.correct: £50,000. You own 1% of the company, so 1% of its profit is yours.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find your fraction of the shares, then take that fraction of the profit.

byKey.one-share: That is the profit for one share, £0.50. You hold 100,000 of them.
byKey.tenth: You took 10%. 100,000 out of 10 million is 1%.
byKey.hundredth: You took 0.1%. 100,000 out of 10 million is 1%.

explain.text: You hold $100{,}000 / 10{,}000{,}000 = 1\%$ of the shares. A share is a claim on a slice of the company's profits and assets. So 1% of the £5 million is yours: £50,000.

screens.title: Paid out or kept
screens.prose: The board decides how much of the £5 million to pay out to shareholders. The rest stays in the company to fund growth. Move the payout.

derive.caption: Payout {{round(payout * 100)}}%: each of the 10 million shares receives {{money(0.5 * payout)}}

screens.question: Set the payout to 40%. How much is paid on each share?

hints.text: At 40%, £2 million is paid out in total.
Share it equally among 10 million shares.

feedback.correct: £0.20 a share. That payment is the **dividend**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the amount paid out by the number of shares.

byKey.eps: That is the whole profit per share, £0.50. Only 40% of it is paid out.
byKey.kept: That is the part kept, per share. You want the part paid out.
byKey.millions: £2 million is the total paid. Divide it among 10 million shares.

explain.text: 40% of £5 million is £2 million, so each share gets a **dividend** of £0.20. The £3 million kept is **retained earnings**, reinvested for the shareholders. Profit per share, £0.50, is **earnings per share**.

screens.title: Three numbers on every quote
screens.prose: Price times shares is the **market capitalisation**: what the market says all the shares are worth. Dividend over price is the **dividend yield**. Price over earnings per share is the **price-to-earnings ratio**, P/E.
screens.question: Fill in the three measures.

hints.text: Each measure is one multiplication or division.
Market cap is $5.20 \times 400$ million.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Market cap is price times shares; the other two divide by the price or into it.

byKey.r0c1: Market cap is the share price times the shares in issue: $5.20 \times 400$.
byKey.r1c1: Dividend yield is the dividend divided by the price: $0.13/5.20$, as a percentage.
byKey.r2c1: P/E is the price divided by the earnings per share: $5.20/0.40$.

explain.text: $5.20 \times 400\text{m} = \text{£}2{,}080\text{m}$. The dividend yield is $0.13/5.20 = 2.5\%$. A P/E of 13 means buyers pay £13 for each £1 of this year's profit.

screens.title: The worst case
screens.prose: You paid £2,080 for 400 shares. The company collapses, owing its lenders £50 million more than everything it owns.
screens.question: What is the most you can lose?

hints.text: Can the lenders come to you for the shortfall?
Shareholders are not liable for the company's debts.
You lose the £2,080 you paid, and no more.

feedback.correct: £2,080. Your shares can fall to zero, but no further.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The company's debts are not yours.

byKey.share-of-debt: You added your share of the shortfall, £50. Shareholders do not owe the company's debts.
byKey.debt: The £50 million is owed by the company, not by its owners.
byKey.nothing: Shareholders are paid last. With debts above assets, the shares are worth nothing, so you lose what you paid.

explain.text: This is **limited liability**: an owner's loss is capped at what they paid for the shares. Lenders are paid first from the assets; shareholders get what is left, here nothing. That cap is why shares can trade freely between strangers.

screens.title: Which share is cheap?
screens.prose: Two companies in the same industry. A friend wants share A because it costs only £2.00.
screens.question: Which share is cheaper for each pound of profit it earns?

options.why: You compared the prices per share. A share of A is a much smaller slice: compare price to earnings.
You may have assumed the market prices both the same. Their P/E ratios differ by a factor of two.
They can: P/E puts both on the same basis, pounds paid per pound of profit.

hints.text: A low price can just mean a small slice of the company.
Divide each price by its earnings per share.

feedback.correct: Share B: a P/E of 10 against 20.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare price to earnings, not price alone.

byKey.a: You compared the prices per share. A share of A is a much smaller slice of its company: its P/E is 20.

explain.text: A costs $2.00/0.10 = 20$ times earnings, B only $50.00/5.00 = 10$ times. The price of one share says nothing about value; it depends on how many shares there are. Compare P/E ratios instead.

screens.title: Dividends for ever
screens.prose: A share will pay £2.00 next year, growing 3% a year after that. Investors want an 8% return. The curve adds up the value today of the first $N$ dividends. Move $N$.

derive.caption: First {{N}} dividends: worth {{money(40*(1 - pow(1.03/1.08, N)))}} today

screens.question: What are all the dividends worth today, if they carry on for ever?

hints.text: Move $N$ far to the right. Does the total keep growing?
Each new dividend adds less than the one before: its value shrinks by $1.03/1.08$.
The total levels off at £40.00.

feedback.correct: £40.00. Infinitely many dividends, but a finite value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Push $N$ to 150 and see where the total levels off.

byKey.no-growth: That is $2/0.08$, which ignores the 3% growth.
byKey.ten: That counts only the first 10 dividends. They carry on for ever.
byKey.plus: That is $2/(0.08 + 0.03)$. Growth makes the share worth more, not less.

explain.text: Each dividend is worth $1.03/1.08 = 0.954$ times the one before it, today. The values shrink, so the total settles: £39.97 after 150 years, £40.00 in the limit. A share is the present value of all its future payouts.

screens.title: Where £40 comes from
screens.prose: Call next year's dividend $D$, its growth rate $g$ and the required return $r$. Each dividend is $1 + g$ times the last, and one more year away.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: A geometric series with first term $a = \dfrac{D}{1+r}$ and ratio $q = \dfrac{1+g}{1+r}$, dividing each term by the one before
When $g < r$, $0 < q < 1$, so the series converges to $\dfrac{a}{1 - q}$
$1 - q = \dfrac{(1+r) - (1+g)}{1+r} = \dfrac{r - g}{1+r}$, over a common denominator

hints.text: Write the price as a sum first.
Find the ratio between neighbouring terms.
Sum, ratio, convergence, simplify $1 - q$, divide.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the sum, name its ratio, then use the infinite geometric sum.

explain.text: This is the infinite geometric sum from the Sequences and Series course: $a/(1 - q)$ with $q = (1+g)/(1+r)$. It is the **dividend discount model**. Its continuous twin, $\int_0^\infty D e^{(g-r)t}\,dt = D/(r - g)$, is an integral that runs to infinity from the Integrals course.

screens.title: What moves a share price
screens.prose: Nothing about the company changes, but interest rates rise and investors now want 10% a year from this share. The curve is $P = 2/(r - 0.03)$.
screens.question: What is the share worth at a 10% required return?

hints.text: Only $r$ changes in $P = D/(r - g)$.

feedback.correct: £28.57, down 29%, with no change in the company.

byKey.same: The dividends are unchanged, but they are now discounted at 10%. The price falls.
byKey.no-growth: That is $2/0.10$, which ignores the 3% growth.
byKey.plus: That adds $g$ to $r$. Growth is subtracted: $r - g$.

explain.text: $2.00/0.07 = \text{£}28.57$, a 29% fall. A share price moves with the cash flows investors expect and the rate they discount them at. Here only the rate moved, as for a bond.

screens.title: Growth too fast
screens.prose: Move the growth rate $g$ towards the 8% required return. The curve is $P = 2/(r - g)$, drawn for $r > g$.

derive.caption: Growth {{fixed(g, 1)}}%: at r = 8%, {{g < 8 ? 'price ' + money(200/(8 - g)) : 'no finite price'}}

screens.question: Set $g$ to 8%, the same as $r$. What does the model say the share is worth?

options.text: It gives no answer: the dividends' values never shrink, so the sum has no limit

options.why: You read dividing by zero as giving zero. The terms do not shrink, so the sum grows without end.

options.text: An infinite amount, so it is worth buying at any price
options.why: You trusted the formula outside its range. No company outgrows the required return for ever: the inputs are wrong.
You dropped the growth. With $g = r$ every term is $2/1.08$, the same for ever.

hints.text: At $g = r$, what is the ratio $q = (1+g)/(1+r)$?
$q = 1$, so every dividend is worth the same today.
A sum of infinitely many equal terms has no limit: the model breaks.

feedback.correct: The model needs $g < r$. At $g \ge r$ the series diverges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the ratio between neighbouring terms when $g = r$.

explain.text: With $g = r$ the ratio is $q = 1$: every dividend is worth £1.85 today, for ever. The sum has no limit, and for $g > r$ it grows faster still. A long-run growth rate above the required return is a sign the inputs are wrong.

screens.title: Valuing a share
screens.prose:
Market cap $= P \times N$, dividend yield $= D/P$, P/E $= P/\text{EPS}$. A share is worth its future payouts, discounted:
$$P = \frac{D}{r - g}, \quad g < r$$
where $D$ is next year's dividend.
screens.question: A company pays no dividend. It reinvests its profit and plans to buy back shares later. What is its share worth?

options.text: The value today of the cash it will return later, as dividends or buybacks

options.why: You set every future payout to zero. Cash can come later, or through buybacks.

options.text: Exactly its assets minus its debts
options.why: That is the book value. The price also counts the profit the assets will earn.

feedback.correct: Payouts can start later or take another form. The share is worth them, discounted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what cash the owners will get, and when.

explain.text: A **buyback** returns cash by buying shares from those who want to sell. A young firm reinvesting at high returns grows its later payouts. $D/(r - g)$ is only the case of payouts starting next year and growing steadily.

screens.title: Reading a company's numbers
screens.prose: An analyst screens a UK retailer. Its shares trade at £3.45. Fill in the measures a screen shows.
screens.question: Fill in the market cap, dividend yield and P/E.

hints.text: Totals work as well as per-share figures: divide total by total.
Market cap is $3.45 \times 1{,}200$ million.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the market cap first; the other two divide by it or into it.

byKey.r1c1: Dividend yield is total dividends over market cap: $124.2/4{,}140$.
byKey.r2c1: P/E is market cap over total profit: $4{,}140/276$.

explain.text: Market cap is $3.45 \times 1{,}200\text{m} = \text{£}4{,}140\text{m}$. Total over total, the dividend yield is 3.0% and the P/E is 15. Buying the whole firm would also take on its debt: that wider price is **enterprise value**.

screens.title: A rights issue
screens.prose: A company's shares trade at £5.00. To raise cash it offers a **rights issue**: one new share at £3.00 for every four held. Every holder takes up the offer.

rows: Cash paid for one new share

screens.question: What should each share trade at afterwards?

hints.text: No value is created or lost: add up what the holder has.
Four shares worth £20.00, plus £3.00 of new cash, now spread over 5 shares.

feedback.correct: £4.60. The holder's total, £23.00, is unchanged by the issue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the old shares' value and the new cash, then divide by 5.

byKey.unchanged: New shares sold at £3.00 bring in less than £5.00 each, so the average price falls.
byKey.average: You averaged £5.00 and £3.00. There are four old shares for each new one.

explain.text: Before: £20.00 of shares plus £3.00 of cash, £23.00. After: 5 shares worth £23.00, so £4.60 each. A share split works the same way: 2-for-1 halves the price and doubles the shares, and value is unchanged.

ideas: A share is a claim on a slice of a company's profits and assets. Losses stop at what you paid.
Market cap is price times shares; dividend yield is $D/P$; P/E is price over earnings per share. Compare P/E, never the price alone.
A share is worth its future payouts discounted: $P = D/(r - g)$ for steady growth with $g < r$. A higher required return lowers the price.

formula.name: Dividend discount model
formula.note: $D$ is next year's dividend. Valid only for $g < r$.

summary.trap: A £2 share is not cheaper than a £50 share. Compare price to earnings.

quiz.prose: A company has 250 million shares in issue, trading at £8.40.
quiz.question: What is its market capitalisation, in £ billion?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the price by the number of shares.

byKey.millions: That is the answer in millions. Give it in billions: 2,100 million is 2.1 billion.
byKey.per-share: That is one share's price. Multiply by 250 million shares.

quiz.prose: You hold 150 shares at £80.00. The company does a 2-for-1 share split.
quiz.question: What are your shares worth straight after the split?

options.why: You doubled the shares but kept the price. Each new share is half an old one.
You halved the price but kept 150 shares. You now hold 300.

feedback.correct: £12,000, as before. A split slices the same company more thinly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A split changes the count and the price, not the value.

explain.text: Each share becomes two, so you hold 300, and each is worth half, £40.00. $300 \times 40 = \text{£}12{,}000 = 150 \times 80$.

quiz.prose: A share will pay a £1.50 dividend next year, growing 4% a year for ever. Investors require 9% a year.
quiz.question: What is it worth?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P = D/(r - g)$.

quiz.prose: A share trades at £40.00 and pays a dividend of £1.20 a year. Its earnings per share are £2.50.
quiz.question: What is its dividend yield?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the dividend by the price.

byKey.earnings: That is earnings over price, $2.50/40$. Use the dividend.
byKey.payout: That is dividend over earnings, the payout ratio. Divide by the price.
